analysis.one_liner: An omnibus bill repealing health coverage protections, income taxes, and abortion access while deregulating silencers and preempting state rules.
analysis.headline: Introduced on the final day of the Congress with zero cosponsors, the bill was referred to 12 House committees and died with no committee action and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill bundles dozens of sweeping changes into one act: it repeals the Affordable Care Act, bans most abortions after a fetal heartbeat is detected and strips federal courts of power to review abortion laws, replaces income, payroll, and estate taxes with a national sales tax, repeals school nutrition standards and federal education law in favor of vouchers, lifts regulation of firearm silencers, lets producers sue to overturn state rules on how agricultural products are made, caps malpractice awards, and imposes mandatory minimums for immigration reentry. It also contains a handful of provisions pitched at families, including school vouchers, tax deductions for health premiums, and expanded savings accounts. It was introduced on the last day the 116th Congress was in session, attracted no cosponsors, and was never considered by any committee or the full House.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the largest gains would flow to high-income households and large estates, who would stop paying income and estate taxes and face a national sales tax instead; gun silencer makers, freed from federal registration and taxation; agricultural producers, who could sue to invalidate state standards on how their products are made; private schools and voucher users; medical providers and their insurers, protected by a $250,000 cap on malpractice damages; intellectual property holders, who would receive tariff proceeds as compensation for losses in China; and food companies, freed from 2012 school lunch nutrition standards.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, large estates, and industry lobbies

how_it_helps.text: Repeals federal income taxes, payroll taxes, and estate and gift taxes and establishes a national sales tax in their place, eliminating taxes that fall most heavily on high incomes and inherited wealth [S2][S3].
Prohibits state and local regulation of firearm silencers and removes silencers from the National Firearms Act's registration and tax scheme [S3].

Creates a private right of action for producers to invalidate any state or local standard or condition on the production of agricultural products sold in interstate commerce, with automatic preliminary injunctions against states that lose the threshold showing [S3].
Caps noneconomic damages at $250,000 in any health care lawsuit and adds procedures limiting malpractice claims, which reduces liability costs for providers and insurers [S2][S3].
Imposes duties on merchandise from China equal to estimated annual revenue losses to U.S. intellectual property holders and pays those proceeds out to rights holders who can document losses [S3].
Repeals the 2012 nutrition standards for school lunches and breakfasts and bars calorie maximums or restrictions on lunches from home [S2][S3].

For some households, it adds a tax deduction for health insurance premiums, expands health savings account contribution limits to $10,000 ($20,000 for couples) without a high-deductible-plan requirement, and permits opting out of Medicare Part A while carrying other coverage [S3].

Repeals the Elementary and Secondary Education Act and converts federal elementary and secondary education spending into block grants funding vouchers that parents can use for private school or homeschooling [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Lower- and middle-income households would bear the brunt of a national sales tax replacing progressive income taxes; the millions of people who gained coverage under the Affordable Care Act would lose that coverage, since the bill pairs repeal only with vouchers, deductions, and savings accounts; abortion patients in most states of pregnancy would lose access, with the exception life-threatening physical conditions; patients injured by malpractice would have awards capped; construction workers on federal projects would lose Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage protection; states and their residents would lose the power to enforce standards on products made elsewhere; and every consumer would pay a new national sales tax on purchases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Lower-income households, patients, and coverage consumers

drawbacks.text: Replacing the income, payroll, and estate tax system with a national sales tax shifts the tax burden downward: sales taxes take a larger share of income from households that spend most of what they earn, while the repeal of income and estate taxes delivers the largest dollar benefit to the highest earners and inheritances [S2][S3].

Repealing the Affordable Care Act without an equivalent coverage guarantee would end protections that keep coverage affordable for people with preexisting conditions and subsidy recipients; the bill's replacement provisions (premium deductions, HSAs, vouchers exist only in education) do not recreate the subsidies, Medicaid expansion, or insurance rules the law contains [S2][S3].

The bill declares fetal personhood from fertilization and strips both the Supreme Court and district courts of jurisdiction over any case challenging a law that protects fetal life or limits abortion, removing ordinary judicial review of state and federal abortion laws [S3].

The private right of action against state production standards, with automatic injunctions, would let out-of-state producers challenge state laws on animal welfare, labeling, and production methods, and the bill's own sponsor framed it against state regulation of agricultural products [S3].

Repealing Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage requirements removes the wage floor for construction workers on federally funded projects, and the bill also makes wages paid to unauthorized workers non-deductible and expands E-Verify, raising compliance costs and employment risk [S3].

Even a supporter would concede the bill is a wish list, not legislation: bundling tax repeal, abortion bans, gun deregulation, education vouchers, immigration penalties, and veterans' wheelchairs into one act means no committee could responsibly examine any of it, which is why it drew no cosponsors [S4][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's costs to ordinary people dominate. The tax rewrite would be the largest upward transfer of its kind, since ending income and estate taxes benefits the highest earners most while a sales tax falls hardest on those who spend everything they make. Repealing the ACA with no replacement coverage mechanism, capping malpractice victims' awards, preempting state standards, and stripping courts of abortion-review jurisdiction each impose real losses on large groups of people. The provisions aimed at working families — premium deductions, larger HSAs, vouchers, veterans' mobility equipment — are modest by comparison and in several cases work best for households that already have income to save. Honest supporters of individual pieces would still have to defend the whole package, which is likely why no member joined it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on the last day of the Congress, sent to twelve committees, and none of them ever acted, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King (R-IA) introduced the bill on December 31, 2020, the final day the 116th Congress was in session [S1][S5].
No member of either party signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The same day, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee and eleven others, including Ways and Means, Appropriations, and Rules [S5].
No committee reported the bill and the House never voted on it; the Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill expired [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so no one gained. The people better off because it died are those it targeted: households with Affordable Care Act coverage, abortion patients, construction workers, states enforcing production standards, and low- and middle-income taxpayers, since a tax rewrite that large would have taken years to unwind.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: ACA holders, abortion patients, and workers, unaffected

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the bill's sole sponsor was a Republican, and it drew zero cosponsors from either party, so support was never tested.

industries.note: Repeal of income, payroll, and estate taxes replaced by a national sales tax would deliver the largest tax cut to the highest earners and inheritances while a sales tax takes the biggest share of income from households that spend nearly everything they earn.

industries.industry: Health insurers and health care providers
industries.note: Repealing the ACA would strip insurers of millions of subsidized customers and undo insurance rules, though the bill adds premium deductions, expanded HSAs, and a malpractice damages cap that lowers provider and insurer liability costs. Patients lose coverage protections in exchange for tax benefits that work best for households with money to save.

The interstate commerce title lets producers sue to invalidate state standards on how products sold across state lines are made, with automatic injunctions against states, weakening state animal-welfare, labeling, and production rules.

The SHUSH Act title removes silencers from National Firearms Act registration and taxation and voids state taxes, registration, and recordkeeping on silencers, expanding the market while reducing oversight.

The voucher title repeals federal education law and funds per-child payments that parents can spend on private tuition or homeschooling, creating a federal customer base for private education while removing money and federal accountability from public school systems.
Tariffs on Chinese goods equal to estimated IP losses would be deposited in a trust fund and paid out to rights holders who document losses — a direct transfer from import consumers to IP owners.

A $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages plus affidavit, expert-witness, and notice requirements would shrink payouts and claims, lowering insurer costs at the direct expense of injured patients' recoveries.
Repealing the 2012 school meal nutrition standards and barring calorie maximums removes the rules that limited sugar, sodium, and processed food in the federal school lunch and breakfast programs.
Repealing Davis-Bacon lets contractors on federally funded projects pay below-prevailing wages, raising contractor margins while cutting construction workers' pay.
